analysis.one_liner: Designates Northern Rockies wildlands as wilderness and bars logging, mining, and drilling there.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 139 House cosponsors — 130 Democrats and 9 Republicans — but after one subcommittee hearing it never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would protect federal public lands across Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming as wilderness — roughly 19 million acres — plus wild and scenic rivers, wildlife connecting corridors, and new land-restoration programs. Roadbuilding, logging, mining, and drilling would be banned on the designated land. It also guarantees Native American tribes access to the areas for traditional cultural and religious uses and funds a restoration jobs corps. The House never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who hunts, fishes, hikes, or drinks water downstream of the Northern Rockies. The bill would protect the headwaters of major rivers, keep wildlife habitat intact, guarantee tribal access for traditional and religious uses, and fund restoration jobs for local businesses [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hunters, anglers, hikers, downstream water users

how_it_helps.text: Designates lands across Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming as wilderness — the seven ecosystem designations total roughly 19.2 million acres — protecting the headwaters of the Columbia, Snake, Green, Missouri, and Saskatchewan river systems that supply farms, cities, and fisheries.
Ends roadbuilding, logging, mining, and drilling on those lands; the bill's findings say current extraction there runs at a loss to taxpayers through below-cost timber sales.
Creates a National Wildland Restoration and Recovery System and a Wildland Recovery Corps to repair damaged lands, providing contracts and work for local businesses and outdoor trades.
Guarantees Native American tribes nonexclusive access to the designated areas for traditional cultural and religious purposes.
Adds river segments in Idaho, Montana, and Wyoming to the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System, protecting trout streams and water quality.

analysis.who_pays: Timber, mining, and oil and gas companies, which would lose access to designated public lands; motorized recreation users, since wilderness bans snowmobiles and ATVs; and rural communities whose work is tied to resource extraction [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber, mining, and oil and gas companies

drawbacks.text: Wilderness designation would permanently bar roadbuilding, timber harvest, mining, and oil and gas drilling on the designated land, ending those economic activities there.
Because the designations ride on the Wilderness Act, motorized access such as snowmobiling and ATV use is prohibited in wilderness areas — a real loss for ordinary recreation users of these lands.
The bill's own findings acknowledge rural, resource-dependent communities in the region; those communities would bear job and revenue losses as extraction ends on the designated acres.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded concentrated, ongoing resource extraction for permanent protection of water, wildlife, and recreation across a vast region, and its restoration corps would have replaced some of the lost extraction jobs with restoration work. The costs would have fallen on specific industries and some rural communities; the benefits — clean water, intact ecosystems, recreation, and tribal access — are broad and lasting. Its main design weakness is scale: one bill locking up roughly 19 million acres across five states drew regional resistance that state-by-state wilderness compromises have historically avoided, and no compromise ever happened here because the bill died in committee.

outcome.mechanism: Its committee held a single hearing, then never voted on the bill, so it died when the two-year Congress ended without any House or Senate vote ever being taken.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney introduced the bill on April 20, 2007; it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources and then to its National Parks, Forests and Public Lands Subcommittee.

The subcommittee held one hearing on October 18, 2007, and then no further action ever occurred — no committee vote, no floor vote, and no Senate action before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
The bill ended the Congress with 139 cosponsors, 130 of them Democrats and 9 of them Republicans.
Under House practice a bill cannot reach the floor until its committee approves it, and no such approval ever happened here, so the outcome was decided inside one committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber, mining, and oil and gas interests kept the affected public lands open to logging, mining, and drilling, and the public received no new wilderness protection from this bill during the 110th Congress.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan backing.

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its National Parks, Forests and Public Lands Subcommittee, held one hearing on October 18, 2007, and never voted to report the bill during the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Timber, mining, and oil and gas industries
against.role: Extractive industries with access to the affected federal lands
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill's expansion of wilderness over lands open to logging, mining, and drilling.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but lopsided — 130 of the 139 cosponsors were Democrats and 9 were Republicans — and the bill died in committee without a roll-call vote, so the chamber never formally recorded a split.

industries.note: Bars timber harvest across roughly 19 million acres of federal forest. The bill's findings describe remaining federal timber sales as below-cost and subsidized by taxpayers, so the industry loses access it was partly getting at the public's expense.
Wilderness designation closes the designated federal lands to mining development, ending future claims across the five-state region.
Removes the designated acres from energy development by barring drilling there.
Protects the hunting, fishing, and wilderness-based recreation economies the bill's findings identify as the region's sustainable economic base, and funds restoration work for local businesses.

industries.industry: Motorized recreation (snowmobile and ATV users and outfitters)
industries.note: Wilderness bans motorized access in the designated areas. Unlike the extractive industries, these users are ordinary members of the public, so their lost access is a genuine public cost of the designations.
